cues.text: Before his mission to England, Augustine served as prior of the monastery of St.

Andrew on Rome's Caelian Hill — the very monastery Pope Gregory the Great had founded on his own family estate before his election to the papacy, placing Augustine among the pope's closest and most trusted monastic associates when Gregory finally set his long-deferred plan to evangelize England into motion.

Around June 596, Augustine set out with some forty monks on the long overland journey toward the English Channel, but discouragement overtook the company before they had gone far: frightening tales of the fierce, uncivilized island people they were bound to evangelize chilled their enthusiasm, and several of the monks proposed turning back rather than risk the uncertain mission ahead.

Augustine, sharing something of his companions' anxiety, agreed to return in person to Rome and lay their fears plainly before Gregory himself, rather than simply overruling his brethren's genuine terror.

Gregory's response was firm but encouraging rather than harsh: he sent Augustine back to his waiting company armed with fresh letters of support, and the mission, its confidence restored, pressed on at last toward Britain.

Augustine and his companions landed on the Isle of Thanet in the kingdom of Kent in 597, where they found conditions more favorable than their earlier fears had led them to expect: King Æthelberht , though himself still pagan, had married a Frankish Christian princess, Bertha , who had been permitted to bring her own chaplain and to practice her faith openly at court — a quiet Christian presence already established, without any missionary effort at all, through one queen's steady, patient fidelity.

Æthelberht received the missionaries cautiously but courteously, meeting them in the open air, tradition holds, out of a superstitious wariness of foreign magic, and, after a period of careful observation of their manner of life, was himself converted and baptized, followed in short order by large numbers of his subjects.

With the king's conversion secured, Augustine was consecrated bishop and established his episcopal seat at Canterbury , the royal capital of Kent, founding there the see that has remained, for fourteen centuries since, the symbolic and historic center of the English Church.

Gregory sent Augustine the pallium — the woolen band signifying full archiepiscopal authority — along with detailed pastoral guidance on organizing the new English Church, including his celebrated counsel that pagan temples, rather than being destroyed outright, might often be more effectively converted to Christian use, and that familiar local customs be adapted rather than abolished wherever this could be done without compromising the faith itself.

Augustine's mission was not without real setbacks: an attempt to establish friendly relations and liturgical unity with the older British Christian communities, descendants of Roman Britain's own earlier Church, ended in mutual mistrust and failure, with the British bishops refusing to recognize Augustine's authority or to adjust their independent customs — a division between the newly established Roman mission and the older native British Church that would persist for generations after Augustine's own death.

Augustine died around 604, having lived to see the foundation of English Christianity firmly established at Canterbury, though the fuller conversion of the whole Anglo-Saxon patchwork of kingdoms would take decades more of labor by his successors.

Remembered as the Apostle of the English , Augustine remains a genuinely reassuring model for every believer who has ever felt nearly overwhelmed by fear before a difficult calling: a missionary who came close to turning back before he had even properly begun, and who became, through nothing more dramatic than a pope's patient encouragement and his own willingness to press forward despite real fear, the founder of a Church that has endured, in an unbroken line from Canterbury, for well over a thousand years.
